sections.title: Will and would: characteristic behaviour, habits, always-true facts
sections.content:
We can use will (for the present) and would (for the past) to talk about –
☆ characteristic behaviour or habits:
• Every day Dan will come home from work and turn on the TV.
• At school she would always sit quietly and pay attention.
☆ things that are or were always true:
• Cold weather will kill certain plants.
• During the war, people would eat all kinds of things that we don't eat now.
(For the use of will to talk about the future, see Unit 9.)
We don't use will or would in this way to talk about a particular occasion. Compare:
• Each time I gave him a problem he would solve it for me. and
• Last night I gave him a problem and he solved it for me. (not … he would solve it …)
However, we can use will not (won't) and would not (wouldn't) in either case. Compare:
• He wouldn't walk the five miles to his place of work. (characteristic behaviour) and
• She wouldn't say what was wrong when I asked her.

sections.title: Stressed will/would for criticism
sections.content:
In speech, we can stress will or would to criticise people's characteristic behaviour or habits:
• She just won't do the washing up when I ask her.
• I was happy when Ryan left. He would talk about people behind their backs.
We can also express disapproval of something they have done using will:
• 'I feel sick.' 'Well, if you will eat so much, I'm not surprised.'

sections.title: Will for conclusions and assumptions
sections.content:
We can use will to draw conclusions or state assumptions about things that are the case now (see also Unit 9B):
• Martina will be at home by now. Let's go and see her.
• You will know that Ewan and Lucy are engaged. (= I assume you already know)

sections.title: Would and used to
sections.content:
When we talk about repeated events in the past that don't happen now we can use either would or used to + infinitive. However, we can use would only if the time reference is clear. Compare:
• We used to play in the garden. (not We would play …; time reference not given) and
• Whenever we went to my uncle's house, we would / used to play in the garden.
Note that negatives and questions are formed with did / didn't + use to (not I didn't used to…).
We can use used to but not would when we talk about past states that have changed:
• The factory used to be over there.
• Didn't you use to have red hair?
We don't use either used to or would when we say exactly how many times in total something happened, how long something took, or that a single event happened at a given past time:
• We visited Switzerland four times during the 1990s. (not We would / used to visit …)
• She went to Jamaica last month. (not She would / used to go to Jamaica last month.)

sections.title: Would/will have + past participle
sections.content:
To talk about an unreal past situation – an imaginary situation or one that might have happened in the past, but didn't – we use would have + past participle:
• I would have been happy to see him, but I didn't have time.
However, to say that we think a past situation actually happened, we use will have + past participle (see also Unit 11C):
• As it was cloudy, few people will have seen last night's lunar eclipse. (rather than … would have seen …)

exercises.question: Most days I ___ eight hours or more in front of my computer.
exercises.hint: Habitual repeated past behaviour → would.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: would spend
We use would here for past habits, hypothetical situations, or reported speech.
💡 Habitual repeated past behaviour → would.

exercises.question: Yesterday I ___ a sharp pain in my lower back.
exercises.hint: Single past occasion → past simple (had).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: had
'Would' and 'used to' both express past habits, but neither can be used for a single event or state on one specific occasion. Use the past simple for individual, completed past moments.

exercises.question: When I was at college, I ___ in the gym most days.
exercises.hint: Habitual past behaviour (time reference 'when I was at college' is clear) → would.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: would exercise
We use would here for past habits, hypothetical situations, or reported speech.
💡 Habitual past behaviour (time reference 'when I was at college' is clear) → would.

exercises.question: When I tried to stand, I ___ that I couldn't straighten up.
exercises.hint: Single past occasion → past simple (found).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: found
'Would' expresses repeated past habits, not single events. A single realisation or discovery at a specific moment requires the past simple.

exercises.question: Over time poor posture ___ back pain.
exercises.hint: Always-true fact → will (present characteristic truth).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will cause
Always-true fact → will (present characteristic truth). Use will here — this is neither a fixed timetable event (which would take the present simple) nor a pre-planned personal arrangement (which would take the present continuous or be going to).

exercises.question: Before computers came along, people ___ rarely ___ still for so long.
exercises.hint: Past habitual behaviour + time reference given → would (or past simple).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was … sitting
Past habitual behaviour + time reference given → would (or past simple). Repeated or habitual actions use the present simple, not the continuous.

exercises.question: I'm sure you ___ about the need to take regular breaks.
exercises.hint: Assumption about what the listener currently knows → will.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will know
Assumption about what the listener currently knows → will. Use will here — this is neither a fixed timetable event (which would take the present simple) nor a pre-planned personal arrangement (which would take the present continuous or be going to).

exercises.question: That ___ probably the result of sitting badly.
exercises.hint: Single past occasion/explanation → past continuous (was causing).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was causing
Single past occasion/explanation → past continuous (was causing). The past continuous here describes an ongoing action that provides the background context for completed past events. It answers "what was happening at that time?" rather than "what happened?".

exercises.question: I would enjoy studying French when I was at school.
options: used to enjoy (state — can't use would)
Both used to enjoy and enjoyed
exercises.hint: 'Enjoy' is a state verb here — can't use 'would'; 'used to enjoy' or 'enjoyed' (past simple) both work.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both used to enjoy and enjoyed
'Enjoy' is a state verb here — can't use 'would'; 'used to enjoy' or 'enjoyed' (past simple) both work. State verbs describe mental states, emotions, or senses and are not normally used in continuous forms.

exercises.question: Jorge would spend winters in Spain and summers in England.
exercises.hint: Habitual pattern without specific count → would spend / used to spend / spent all possible.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both would spend and used to spend are possible
We use would here for past habits, hypothetical situations, or reported speech.
💡 Habitual pattern without specific count → would spend / used to spend / spent all possible.
acceptable: Both would spend and used to spend are possible

exercises.question: We would live in a bungalow on the south coast, and then we moved to a flat in town.
options: used to live (state — would not used for states)
Both would live and used to live
exercises.hint: Living somewhere = state → can't use 'would'; used to live or lived.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: used to live (state — would not used for states)
We use would here for past habits, hypothetical situations, or reported speech.
💡 Living somewhere = state → can't use 'would'; used to live or lived.

exercises.question: On Saturdays and Sundays the ferry used to take tourists across to the island.
exercises.answer: would take (habitual past with clear time ref)
acceptable: Both would take and used to take are correct
exercises.hint: Habitual past → both would take and used to take are correct.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both would take and used to take are correct
We use would here for past habits, hypothetical situations, or reported speech.
💡 Habitual past → both would take and used to take are correct.

exercises.question: The committee would meet four times last week.
options: met (specific count 'four times' → past simple only)
exercises.hint: Specific count ('four times') → neither would nor used to; use past simple (met).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: met (specific count 'four times' → past simple only)
Specific count ('four times') → neither would nor used to; use past simple (met). The past simple requires a specific completed time; present perfect is used when the time is unspecified or the result matters now.

exercises.question: According to official figures, over half the population ___ the final of the song contest on TV last night.
options: will have watched (assumed to be true)
exercises.hint: Assumption that it actually happened → will have watched.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will have watched (assumed to be true)
Assumption that it actually happened → will have watched. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: I enjoyed the exhibition – but I don't think my grandmother ___ of it.
options: would have heard (imaginary — she didn't go)
exercises.hint: Hypothetical/imaginary past — she didn't go → would have heard.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: would have heard (imaginary — she didn't go)
We use would here for past habits, hypothetical situations, or reported speech.
💡 Hypothetical/imaginary past — she didn't go → would have heard.

exercises.question: I don't think the dog ___ anyone, but I was still glad when the owner took it away.
exercises.hint: Imaginary — the dog didn't hurt anyone → would have hurt.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: would have hurt (imaginary situation)
Imaginary — the dog didn't hurt anyone → would have hurt. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: I'm sure by now you ___ about yesterday's robbery at the supermarket.
options: will have heard (assumption that it's true)
exercises.hint: Assumption about current state of knowledge → will have heard.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will have heard (assumption that it's true)
Assumption about current state of knowledge → will have heard. Use will here — this is neither a fixed timetable event (which would take the present simple) nor a pre-planned personal arrangement (which would take the present continuous or be going to).

exercises.question: The train journey was quite comfortable, although I ___ to fly.
exercises.hint: Imaginary preference → would have preferred.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: would have preferred (unreal preference)
Imaginary preference → would have preferred. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: Did you like the present Justin gave you? Well, an umbrella stand isn't something I ___ myself.
options: will have preferred (reviewer assumes it's actually not preferred)
exercises.hint: Expressing an imaginary stronger/different preference → would have preferred.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: would have preferred
Expressing an imaginary stronger/different preference → would have preferred. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: A: I waste so much time looking for parking spaces. B: Well, if you ___, it's a normal thing to happen.
exercises.hint: Expressing disapproval of habitual behaviour → stressed 'will' + infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will arrive late
Expressing disapproval of habitual behaviour → stressed 'will' + infinitive. Use will here — this is neither a fixed timetable event (which would take the present simple) nor a pre-planned personal arrangement (which would take the present continuous or be going to).

exercises.question: A: I've got a headache. B: Well, if you ___, I'm not so surprised.
options: used to stay up at night
exercises.hint: Expressing disapproval of habitual behaviour → stressed 'will'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will stay up at night
Expressing disapproval of habitual behaviour → stressed 'will'. Use will here — this is neither a fixed timetable event (which would take the present simple) nor a pre-planned personal arrangement (which would take the present continuous or be going to).

exercises.question: A: I'm really hot. B: Well, if you ___, it's not a big thing.
exercises.hint: Expressing disapproval/criticism using stressed 'will'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will live in Asia
Expressing disapproval/criticism using stressed 'will'. Use will here — this is neither a fixed timetable event (which would take the present simple) nor a pre-planned personal arrangement (which would take the present continuous or be going to).

exercises.sentence: When I was a child, I would live near the sea.
exercises.correction: When I was a child, I lived near the sea.
acceptable: I used to live near the sea
exercises.hint: 'Would' cannot replace 'used to' for past states — only past repeated actions.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: I lived near the sea
'Would' describes repeated past habits/actions but cannot be used for past states (living somewhere, being something, having something). For past states, use 'used to' or the past simple.

exercises.sentence: She used to can speak three languages before the accident.
exercises.correction: She used to be able to speak three languages before the accident.
acceptable: She was able to speak three languages
exercises.hint: 'Used to can' is not possible — use 'used to be able to' or 'could'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: She used to be able to speak
'Used to' must be followed by a base infinitive. Since 'can' is a modal (not a base infinitive), use 'be able to' instead: 'used to be able to + base verb'.

exercises.sentence: He will always complain about everything — it's just his character.
exercises.correction: He will always complain about everything — it's just his character.
acceptable: He will always complain about everything — it's just his character.
exercises.hint: 'Will + always + verb' expressing characteristic behaviour is correct.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: He will always complain — CORRECT
'Will' + adverb of frequency (always, often, sometimes) expresses characteristic or predictable behaviour. This use of 'will' is correct and is not about the future — it describes a habitual present tendency.
exercises.prompt: Is this sentence correct? If not, rewrite it correctly.
Make a sentence using 'would' to describe a past habit:
exercises.hint: Subject + would + base verb + place + time expression
exercises.explanation:
Answer: She would jog through the park every morning
'Would + base infinitive' describes a repeated past habit. The natural word order places the verb phrase before place, then time: she (subject) + would jog (habit) + through the park (place) + every morning (time).
